# Cantrip

The way in, and the values everything else is written in: `CardRuntime`, `ActionResult`, `Num`.

Part of [the API reference](README.md). The guides are [docs/csharp.md](../csharp.md) and [docs/godot.md](../godot.md); when something here surprises you, [docs/troubleshooting.md](../troubleshooting.md) is the other end of it.

| Type | |
|---|---|
| [`ActionResult`](#actionresult) | What a top-level action did. Every call that can stop for a choice reports it here: `CardRuntime.Play(Entity, Entity, Entity)`, `CardRuntime.StartBattle(bool, bool, string)`, `CardRuntime.EndTurn`, `CardRuntime.Execute(string, Entity, Entity)`, `CardRuntime.UseAbility(Entity, Entity)` and `CardRuntime.Answer(int[])`. |
| [`CardRuntime`](#cardruntime) | The entry point for games: load content, set up actors and decks, then drive battles through `CardRuntime.StartBattle(bool, bool, string)`, `CardRuntime.Play(Entity, Entity, Entity)` and `CardRuntime.EndTurn`, or real-time play through `CardRuntime.Tick(int)` and `CardRuntime.UseAbility(Entity, Entity)`. |
| [`CardRuntime.ReloadReport`](#cardruntimereloadreport) | What `CardRuntime.ApplyContentChanges` did, for tools and logs. |
| [`EntityKind`](#entitykind) | What an entity is. Everything in the game is an entity; this only affects defaults. |
| [`EventPhase`](#eventphase) | The three phases every verb emits: before, instead and after. |
| [`ExecutionMode`](#executionmode) | Pacing of the action queue. |
| [`ModifierLayer`](#modifierlayer) | Fixed layers of the modifier pipeline. Values pass through them in the order the ruleset declares (add, multiply, clamp, override by default), which is what keeps a stack of modifiers from depending on the order they happened to be applied in. |
| [`Num`](#num) | Fixed-point number used for every value the rules engine computes. |
| [`Rng`](#rng) | Deterministic random number generator (xoshiro256** seeded through splitmix64). |
| [`RuntimeOptions`](#runtimeoptions) | *Undocumented.* |
| [`StackingMode`](#stackingmode) | How repeated applications of the same status combine. |
| [`Team`](#team) | Which side an actor is on. Kept deliberately simple; games can layer factions on top. |

## ActionResult

```csharp
public enum ActionResult
```

What a top-level action did. Every call that can stop for a choice reports it here: `CardRuntime.Play(Entity, Entity, Entity)`, `CardRuntime.StartBattle(bool, bool, string)`, `CardRuntime.EndTurn`, `CardRuntime.Execute(string, Entity, Entity)`, `CardRuntime.UseAbility(Entity, Entity)` and `CardRuntime.Answer(int[])`.

| Member | |
|---|---|
| `Played = 0` | The action ran to the end. For `CardRuntime.Play(Entity, Entity, Entity)`, the card was played. |
| `NotACard = 1` | There is nothing to act on: the entity is not a card, or not an ability, or it has been removed, or the actor it belongs to is dead. |
| `NotInHand = 2` | The card is not where it would have to be to be played: not in hand, or not in the pile a `from` named. It is also what `CardRuntime.Play(string, Entity, Entity)` answers when nothing in hand is called that. |
| `Unplayable = 3` | The card is tagged `unplayable` — a curse, a wound, a status card — so no hand it is in ever offers it. Never being playable is the whole of what it is, which is why `cantrip sim` leaves one out of its "held but never playable" finding. |
| `NotEnoughEnergy = 4` | The card costs more of its resource than the actor has. An ability has no cost, so `CardRuntime.UseAbility(Entity, Entity)` never answers this; see `ActionResult.NotReady`. |
| `InvalidTarget = 5` | Nothing legal to aim at. It is one answer for four different refusals, and telling them apart means asking `CardRuntime.LegalTargets(Entity)` what was left: the target given is not among them; the card's own `target ... where` excluded everything; a taunt drew targeting elsewhere; or the side it asks for has nobody alive on it. On a board it is most often `range`: the card cannot reach from where its side stands. |
| `Cancelled = 6` | A `choose` or `discover` was answered with nothing, or the game called `CardRuntime.CancelPending`. The action was rolled back, so nothing it had already done stands. |
| `ChoicePending = 7` | The action needs a decision from the player. The game has been rolled back to where it was; see `CardRuntime.Pending` and answer with `CardRuntime.Answer(int[])`. |
| `NotReady = 8` | An ability that is still on cooldown. See `CardRuntime.IsReady(Entity)`. |

## CardRuntime

```csharp
public sealed class CardRuntime : IDisposable
```

The entry point for games: load content, set up actors and decks, then drive battles through `CardRuntime.StartBattle(bool, bool, string)`, `CardRuntime.Play(Entity, Entity, Entity)` and `CardRuntime.EndTurn`, or real-time play through `CardRuntime.Tick(int)` and `CardRuntime.UseAbility(Entity, Entity)`.


*Undocumented.*

### Properties

```csharp
public Entity? ActiveMember { get; }
```

Whose step it is, or null when the turn order has no single answer. `turns: sides`, the only mode this release has, gives the whole party one turn and lets the game act with its members in any order, so it is always null there and a game asks `CardRuntime.CanAct(Entity)` of each member instead.

```csharp
public bool CanCapture { get; }
```

Whether `CardRuntime.Capture` would succeed right now, so a UI can grey out its save button instead of catching an exception. It is false while effects are still resolving, since snapshots are only valid between actions (a host callback that runs in the middle of a card's effect sees it false too), and while a `next turn:` or `in N turns:` block is waiting whose statements a save cannot hold: one a reload has changed since it was scheduled, or one game code parsed and ran itself rather than through `CardRuntime.Execute(string, Entity, Entity)`. Such a block stops blocking saves once it has run.

```csharp
public IChoiceProvider Chooser { get; set; }
```

Who answers a choice content asks for. Setting it to null throws rather than quietly putting a `FirstOptionChooser` in its place: a game that meant to install its own UI and handed in a null would otherwise find every decision made for it.

The party's dead, in the order they fell — what `CardRuntime.Party` and `State.Actors` leave out, and what content calls `fallen`.

A run that offers to raise a fallen member used to have to keep its own list of member ids from the moment it created them, save it, version it and keep it in step with the snapshot, because a corpse was in none of `Party`, `State.Actors` or the content groups. It is in the snapshot like everyone else; only the way to ask was missing.

The living members of the party, in the order they take their steps. A game that never declares a `hero` has one member: `CardRuntime.Player`.


The decision a UI still has to make, set when an action returned `ActionResult.ChoicePending`. Null when nothing is waiting.

```csharp
public Entity Player { get; }
```

The party's leader: the actor `CardRuntime.CreatePlayer(string, int, int)` made, who holds the run's deck, relics and gold.

**Throws.**

- `InvalidOperationException` — Before `CardRuntime.CreatePlayer(string, int, int)`. Every other call that needs a player needs it too, so the window in which this is empty is the few lines between building a runtime and setting the game up — and a game that asks in that window has its order wrong rather than a player that might not be there.

Not nullable, deliberately. It used to be, and a host with `<Nullable>enable</Nullable>` — which this repository's own `Directory.Build.props` sets, with `WarningsAsErrors=nullable` — could not write `runtime.Player.GetInt("hp")`, the line the guide gives, without a `!` the guide never mentions. `CardRuntime.HasPlayer` is the question worth asking, and it is asked once, at setup.

```csharp
public IReadOnlyList<Entity> AbilitiesOf(Entity owner)
```

The abilities an actor is carrying, in the order they were granted: the row of buttons a real-time front end draws.

An ability is an entity in `Zones.Attached` whose `Entity.Kind` is `EntityKind.Ability`, which is a true sentence that a game should not have to learn: none of the zones the C# guide lists holds an ability, so the only way to list them was to read the assembly.

```csharp
public CardRuntime.ReloadReport ApplyContentChanges()
```

Rebinds every live entity to the definition now loaded under its kind and name, so edits to content take effect in a running game. Call it after reloading files into `CardRuntime.Content`.

Stats the game has changed keep their values; stats still at the old definition's number take the new one. An entity whose definition has disappeared keeps the one it has and is listed in the report.

```csharp
public bool CanAct(Entity member)
```

Whether this member still has its step this round: it is a member, it is alive, a battle is running, and it has not passed. Under `turns: sides` it also has to be the party's turn; under `turns: initiative` it has to be this member's own step, because there the order is the rule rather than a suggestion.

```csharp
public bool CanPlay(Entity card)
```

Whether `CardRuntime.Play(Entity, Entity, Entity)` would accept this card now, aimed somewhere legal: it is in hand, playable, affordable, and a card that needs someone to point at has someone. Content can still cancel it while it resolves, which no check made in advance can see.

```csharp
public bool CanUse(Entity ability)
```

Whether `CardRuntime.UseAbility(Entity, Entity)` would accept this ability now: it is an ability, its owner is alive, it is off cooldown, and one that needs somebody to point at has somebody. The companion of `CardRuntime.CanPlay(Entity)`, and the answer a UI greys a button out on.

```csharp
public void CancelPending()
```

Abandons the pending choice. The game is already back where it was before the action that asked, so nothing else has to be undone.


Captures the full rules state. Only valid between actions; the returned object is plain data that any serializer can store. Throws `InvalidOperationException` whenever `CardRuntime.CanCapture` is false.

```csharp
public Entity CreatePlayer(string name = "Player", int hp = 80, int maxEnergy = 3)
```

*Undocumented.*

```csharp
public void Dispose()
```

Lets go of the clock. A runtime listens to `IGameClock.Advanced` from the moment it is built, which is how scheduled work, periodic triggers and timed statuses run; until it lets go, the clock holds it alive and keeps driving it.

It only matters when a game passes its own clock in `RuntimeOptions.Clock` and outlives a runtime that used it — two runtimes sharing one clock both keep running, and the one nobody uses any more goes on resolving effects on a game that has been replaced. A runtime that made its own clock is collected with it, so nothing is leaked by not calling this. Nothing else is torn down: the state, the content and the entities are ordinary objects, and calling any other member afterwards still works, minus the clock. Calling it twice does nothing the second time.

```csharp
public ActionResult EndBattle(bool won)
```

Ends the running battle, won or lost, as though the last enemy had just fallen: `battle_end` is raised, temporary statuses end, cards go home and `CardRuntime.Won` answers.

**Returns.** `ActionResult.Played`, `ActionResult.Unplayable` when no battle is running, or `ActionResult.ChoicePending` when a `battle_end` effect stops to ask the player something.

The companion of `ends: called`: a game that has turned the automatic ending off needs a way to say the fight is over, and a wave game's ending is a rule of the game above the fight — a timer ran out, a boss arrived, the gate held. It works under `BattleEnd.LastEnemy` too, for a retreat or a surrender.

```csharp
public ActionResult EndTurn()
```

Ends the player's turn, runs the enemies' turn, and starts the next player turn.

**Returns.** `ActionResult.Played`, or `ActionResult.ChoicePending` when something in the turn asks the player to choose: the whole call, enemy turn included, is rolled back and runs again from `CardRuntime.Answer(int[])`.

**Throws.**

- `InvalidOperationException` — This runtime uses a `TickClock`, so it has no turns to end.

```csharp
public ActionResult Execute(string statements, Entity? self = null, Entity? target = null)
```

Runs DSL statements directly, as the REPL and tests do: `runtime.Execute("deal 5 to enemy")`. A `next turn:` or `in N turns:` block among them is saved with their text, so a snapshot taken while it waits restores whatever content is loaded.

**Returns.** `ActionResult.Played`, or `ActionResult.ChoicePending` when the statements ask the player something: they are rolled back and run again from `CardRuntime.Answer(int[])`.

```csharp
public static CardRuntime FromText(string text, RuntimeOptions? options = null)
```

Loads content from text and throws if it has any errors.

```csharp
public IReadOnlyList<Entity> LegalTargets(Entity action)
```

The entities this action may be pointed at right now, in board order, after its own `target … where` filter and content's `targetable` rules: exactly what `CardRuntime.Play(Entity, Entity, Entity)` and `CardRuntime.UseAbility(Entity, Entity)` accept. Empty for one that takes no target. A `target any` action may also be played at nothing, which this list cannot say, so a UI that wants to offer that asks `CardRuntime.TargetMode(Entity)`.

**Parameters.**

- `action` — A card or an ability.

```csharp
public static BlockNode ParseStatements(string statements, string file = "<execute>")
```

Parses free-standing statements by wrapping them in a synthetic block.

```csharp
public ActionResult Pass(Entity member)
```

That member is done for this turn. When the last one that could act has passed, the party's turn ends and the enemies take theirs — so for a party of one this is `CardRuntime.EndTurn`, to the byte.

**Returns.** `ActionResult.Played`, or `ActionResult.ChoicePending` when the turn it ended stopped to ask the player something.

It is a verb of its own rather than an `EndTurn(member)` overload because "end turn" already means "end the side's turn" in the tests, the reference and the Godot node, and one word meaning two things is exactly the silent break a frozen API cannot afford.

```csharp
public bool Place(Entity actor, int lane, int rank)
```

Stands an actor at `lane`, `rank`, raising `moved` so content hears it and `before_moved` can refuse it. The same move content writes as `target.rank = 0`, from C#.

**Returns.** True when the actor stands there afterwards; false when a `before_moved` listener refused the move.

Where somebody stands is a rule and not a view, so the Godot node has nothing that does this — but a rule still has to be reachable from the game that owns the fight above it. A host with waves to place had to execute a string of content for every spawn, which turned a typo in a lane number from a compile error into a `DslException` on a hot path. A slot off the board is refused here with the board's own name and shape, rather than clamped: a wave walking in at a rank that does not exist is a bug in the schedule, and quietly standing it somewhere else would hide it.

```csharp
public ActionResult Play(Entity card, Entity? target = null, Entity? performer = null)
```

Plays a card from hand: checks energy and target, pays, resolves, and drains triggers.

**Parameters.**

- `card` — The card to play, from whichever member's hand it is in.
- `target` — Who it is aimed at, or null to settle from the card's `target` line.
- `performer` — The member doing it, or null for the card's own controller — which is what every game before a party existed means, and what a party of one always has.

The cost is paid by the card's controller, because that is whose pool the card is in. Everything else is the performer's: `card_played.source` is the performer, the damage comes from the performer, `source:` filters match the performer, and the performer's own statuses and modifiers apply. A card that draws draws into the performer's pile, so a member with no pile of its own draws nothing — which is the same sentence as the rule that gave it the party's hand to play from.

```csharp
public ActionResult Play(string cardName, Entity? target = null, Entity? performer = null)
```

Plays the first card of that name in hand, for a game that thinks in names.

**Parameters.**

- `cardName` — The card to look for, matched without regard to case.
- `target` — What to aim it at, or null for one that needs no target.
- `performer` — The member making the play, or null for the card's controller. The card is looked for in that member's own hand first and then in the party's, which is the leader's — the same two shapes a party can take, told apart by whether the member has a hand at all.

```csharp
public long ReadyIn(Entity ability)
```

How much longer this ability has to wait, in clock units: ticks on a `TickClock`, turns on a `TurnClock`. Zero when it is ready.

The number a cooldown sweep is drawn from, and the whole of how a real-time game communicates. Divide by `TickClock.TicksPerSecond` for the seconds a player reads. The answer used to live in an undocumented `ready_at` stat that does not exist at all until the ability has been used once, so a front end had to find the stat by reflection and then know to treat "absent" as ready rather than as zero seconds left.

```csharp
public void RegisterVerb(string name, VerbHandler handler)
```

*Undocumented.*

```csharp
public bool RemoveCard(Entity card)
```

Takes a card out of the game for good, as `destroy` does in content: the way to remove a card from the deck between battles, or to swap one for its upgraded definition. Content hears it as `destroyed`.

**Returns.** Whether the card is gone. False, having changed nothing, for anything that is not a card still in the game.

The Godot node has had this since the addon shipped, with a worked `upgrade_card` recipe beside it, while C# was told to write `Execute("destroy target", target: card)` — the same operation as a typed call on one side of the engine and a parsed string on the other.

```csharp
public void Restore(GameSnapshot snapshot)
```

Replaces the current state with a snapshot. The runtime must have the same content loaded; the next inputs then play out exactly as they would have in the original game. A choice left pending is abandoned: it belonged to the game being replaced.

Everything the snapshot needs is looked up before anything changes, so when it throws `InvalidOperationException`, because a definition the snapshot names is not loaded or a block waiting in it has changed, the game in progress is left as it was.

```csharp
public bool Revive(Entity actor, int hp = 1)
```

Brings a fallen actor back at `hp` hp, raising `revived`. Content writes `revive Vestal 10`; this is the same thing from C#.

**Returns.** True when the actor is alive afterwards. False for one that was never dead.

It exists because `heal` refuses a dead target, deliberately, and so there was no way at all to put a fallen party member back on its feet.

```csharp
public void RollIntent(Entity enemy)
```

Picks an enemy's next move from its pattern, so the UI can show intents in advance.

```csharp
public Num SetStat(Entity entity, string stat, long value)
```

Sets a stat on an actor, or on a card: the same thing content's `speed = 6` does, with the resource's own bounds, the `<stat>_changed` event, and death when hp reaches zero. Returns the change that was actually applied, which a bound or a listener may have cut short.

There was no typed way to write a number onto an entity at all, so a game that finished creating its leader — a `speed` for `order: speed`, a starting shard count — or spent gold in a shop had to build a statement and call `Execute`: `runtime.Execute($"lose {amount} gold")`, a string-interpolated statement, unchecked until it runs, for subtracting an integer.

```csharp
public Entity SpawnEnemy(string name, int? hp = null)
```

Puts an enemy on the board and announces it with `created`, the same event content's own `create` raises.

The event is an announcement rather than a gate: the enemy is already in the game when it is raised, so a `before created:` listener cannot stop a spawn the host has decided on. What it buys is the thing a wave game needs and had no way to write — an arrival effect, a self-placement, a relic that hears anything entering the fight: `on created(target:self): self.rank = 3` on the enemy's own declaration. In a turn game a spawn happens once, before the battle, so this never came up; in a real-time game it is the most frequent event there is.

```csharp
public ActionResult StartBattle(bool shuffle = true, bool drawOpeningHand = true, string? board = null)
```

*Undocumented.*

**Parameters.**

- `shuffle` — Shuffle the draw pile first. Tests turn this off to control draw order.
- `drawOpeningHand` — Draw the first hand. Tests turn this off to set the hand explicitly.
- `board` — The board to fight this battle on, by name, or null to keep the one in play — which before the first battle is `ContentLibrary.DefaultBoard`. Content owns the shapes: a name no `board` declaration matches is refused rather than invented, because the linter has to know how deep a board is to check what reaches across it.

**Returns.** `ActionResult.Played`, or `ActionResult.ChoicePending` when a `battle_start` effect asks the player something: the whole call is rolled back and runs again from `CardRuntime.Answer(int[])`.

```csharp
public string TargetMode(Entity action)
```

What an action asks to be aimed at: `enemy`, `ally`, `self`, `any`, or `none` for one with no `target` line. A card or an ability; both read their `target` line the same way.

```csharp
public void Tick(int count = 1)
```

Advances a `TickClock`. Call from the engine's fixed timestep.

```csharp
public ActionResult UseAbility(Entity ability, Entity? target = null)
```

Uses an ability if it is off cooldown.

**Returns.** `ActionResult.Played` when it ran, `ActionResult.NotReady` while it is still on cooldown, `ActionResult.NotACard` when the ability has been removed or its owner is gone or dead, and `ActionResult.ChoicePending` when it stopped to ask the player something.

An ability reads its own `target` line exactly as a card does, so `ActionResult.InvalidTarget` means the same here as there: an ability that asks for an enemy and has none left is refused rather than run at nobody. An ability has no cost, so it still never answers `ActionResult.NotEnoughEnergy`; that one is here for the day it does, so adding it is not a change to this signature.

## EventPhase

```csharp
public enum EventPhase
```

The three phases every verb emits: before, instead and after.

| Member | |
|---|---|
| `Before = 0` | Runs before the action, and may cancel or alter its inputs. |
| `Instead = 1` | Replaces the action entirely: prevention, redirection, conversion. |
| `After = 2` | Runs after the action has resolved. The common case. |

---

## ExecutionMode

```csharp
public enum ExecutionMode
```

Pacing of the action queue.

| Member | |
|---|---|
| `Headless = 0` | Drain the queue as fast as possible. Used by simulations and tests. |
| `Live = 1` | Yield between actions so presentation can keep up. |

## Num

```csharp
public struct Num : IComparable<Num>, IEquatable<Num>, IFormattable
```

Fixed-point number used for every value the rules engine computes.

The core never uses `Single` or `Double`. Replays, tests, saves and headless balance runs rely on the same content, seed and inputs producing the same game on every machine, within one version of Cantrip, and IEEE floating point does not promise that once a JIT is allowed to contract or reorder operations.

Values are stored as a `Int64` scaled by `Num.Scale` (one millionth), which makes percentages and the usual 0.5 / 1.5 / 0.25 multipliers exact. Multiplication and division are written to avoid 64-bit overflow for any value in the +/- 1,000,000 range, which is far beyond what game numbers need.

```csharp
public long ToLong()
```

Rounds half away from zero and returns the result as a `Int64`, for the values that are counts of clock units rather than damage.

A cast does not work and cannot be made to: `(long)entity.Get("ready_at")` is `CS0030`, because a `Num` is a fixed-point number and not a `Int64` in disguise. `Num.ToInt` is the usual answer and `Num.ToDouble` keeps the fraction; this is the one in between, for a tick count that outgrows an `Int32`.

## Rng

```csharp
public sealed class Rng
```

Deterministic random number generator (xoshiro256** seeded through splitmix64).

`Random` is explicitly not usable here: its algorithm is not guaranteed stable across .NET versions, so a replay recorded on one build could diverge on the next. This implementation is pure integer arithmetic with a small, fully serializable state, so `seed + input log` reproduces any bug exactly.

### Constructors



### Methods


Rolls against a percentage, so `Chance(30)` is true 30% of the time.

```csharp
public Rng Fork(ulong salt)
```

Creates an independent stream derived from this generator, so that (for example) card shuffles and enemy AI rolls cannot perturb each other's sequences.

```csharp
public ulong[] GetState()
```

Snapshot of the full generator state, for save games and replays: four words, in the same order and shape `GameSnapshot.Rng` writes them.

An array rather than a tuple because a tuple's arity is part of its type: a generator with a fifth word would be a breaking change to every caller, and a save already carries this state as a list of words alongside the generator's name.


The run's seed. Any 64-bit number is a seed of its own, 0 and negative ones included, so a host can hand it whatever number it computed.

It used to be `ulong`, which compiled for the literal the guide shows and for nothing a host works out for itself: every game that seeded a run from an `int` wrote `(ulong)(uint)seed`, and Godot's own seed export is signed.

## StackingMode

```csharp
public enum StackingMode
```

How repeated applications of the same status combine.

| Member | |
|---|---|
| `Intensity = 0` | Stacks add up; there is no timer. Poison, Strength. |
| `Duration = 1` | Duration extends; intensity is fixed. Most timed buffs. |
| `Both = 2` | Both stacks and duration accumulate. |
| `None = 3` | Reapplying does nothing while it is already present. |
| `Refresh = 4` | Reapplying resets the duration to full rather than extending it. |
| `Separate = 5` | Each application is tracked as its own instance, with its own source and timer. |
